title: Reactivity of Coordination Compounds
description: Ligand substitution mechanisms, lability and inertness, the trans effect, and electron-transfer reactions.
overview: Stability and reactivity are different questions. A complex that is thermodynamically very stable can still exchange its ligands in microseconds, and one that is thermodynamically unstable can persist for years. The cobalt(III) ammines that Werner studied were hardly known to react, and that inertness is why their isomers could be separated. How fast a complex changes depends on its d-electron count, geometry and the pathway it follows.

This chapter deals with the rates and mechanisms of ligand substitution in octahedral and square planar complexes, the trans effect that guides the synthesis of platinum drugs, and the electron-transfer reactions between complexes, including Marcus theory.
objectives: Distinguish labile from inert complexes, and relate lability to d-electron configuration.
Describe the dissociative, associative and interchange mechanisms, and how experiments tell them apart.
Write the Eigen–Wilkins mechanism and the SN1CB mechanism of base hydrolysis.
Explain substitution in square planar complexes and apply the trans effect to synthesize cis- and trans-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂].
Distinguish inner-sphere from outer-sphere electron transfer, and apply the Marcus cross relation.

sections.title: Labile and inert complexes
body: A **ligand substitution** replaces one ligand with another: [ML₅X] + Y → [ML₅Y] + X. Taube’s classification calls a complex **labile** if substitution is complete within about a minute at 25 °C (0.1 M solutions), and **inert** if it is slower. These are kinetic terms that must not be confused with thermodynamic stability: [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is thermodynamically unstable toward aqueous acid (K for the hydrolysis is about 10²⁵) but survives for days because the reaction is so slow, whereas the very stable [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ exchanges its cyanide quickly.
The rate of water exchange in [M(H₂O)₆]ⁿ⁺ is a convenient measure, and the d-electron count explains the pattern:

The pattern is explained by the **ligand field activation energy**, the loss of LFSE when the complex moves to the transition state, a five-coordinate square pyramid (dissociative) or a seven-coordinate pentagonal bipyramid (associative). Complexes with large LFSE in the octahedral ground state lose more on activation and are inert: **d³ (Cr³⁺, V²⁺) and low-spin d⁶ (Co³⁺, Rh³⁺, Ir³⁺, Fe(II) with CN⁻) are inert**, and so are low-spin d⁴, d⁵ and, with strong fields, d⁸. High-spin d⁴ and d⁹ complexes (Jahn–Teller distortion gives weak axial bonds), and d⁰, d¹, d², d⁵ (high spin) and d¹⁰ ions, are labile. Heavier metals (4d, 5d) are more inert than 3d metals because of their larger Δ and stronger bonds.

check.q: Can a thermodynamically unstable complex be inert?
check.a: Yes, if the reaction is kinetically slow
wrong: No, instability means a fast reaction

sections.title: Substitution mechanisms in octahedral complexes
body: Substitution mechanisms are classified by the transition state.

list: **Dissociative (D)**: the leaving group departs first, giving a five-coordinate intermediate of lower coordination number, which then captures the entering group (like SN1).

**Associative (A)**: the entering group attaches first, giving a seven-coordinate intermediate (like SN2). It is uncommon for octahedral complexes of the first row, but more common for large 4d and 5d metals.

**Interchange (I)**: no detectable intermediate. The entering and leaving groups exchange in a single step within an outer-sphere complex. If bond breaking dominates it is **Iₐ** (associative interchange) when bond making matters and **I_d** (dissociative interchange) when bond breaking leads. Most octahedral substitutions are **I_d**.

body: For octahedral complexes in water, the **Eigen–Wilkins mechanism** is the general model. The entering ligand Y first forms an outer-sphere ion pair with the complex in a rapid equilibrium (constant K_os, which depends on charges and size, about 0.1–10 M⁻¹), and the interchange step (rate constant k) then occurs within the pair:

At low [Y] the rate is first order in Y, and at high [Y] it levels off (saturation), when all the complex is in the ion pair. In the saturated limit the rate no longer depends on the nature of Y, which is evidence for a dissociative interchange: the rate depends on how easily the leaving group departs. The **activation volume** ΔV‡ also distinguishes: positive for dissociative pathways (the transition state is larger than the reactants, as the leaving group moves away), negative for associative.

Ammine complexes of Co(III) hydrolyze in base according to rate = k[complex][OH⁻], though OH⁻ does not attack the metal directly. The **SN1CB** (substitution, nucleophilic, unimolecular, conjugate base) mechanism accounts for this: hydroxide first deprotonates a coordinated NH₃ in a fast equilibrium to give the amido complex [Co(NH₃)₄(NH₂)Cl]⁺. The amido ligand is a strong π-donor and labilizes the loss of chloride, giving a five-coordinate intermediate captured by water. The reaction is 10⁶ times faster than in neutral solution, and it only occurs for complexes with N–H groups.

sections.title: Square planar substitution and the trans effect
terms: associative substitution in square planar complexes
body: Square planar d⁸ complexes (Pt(II), Pd(II), Au(III), Ni(II) with strong ligands) are open to attack from above and below the plane, so they react by an **associative** mechanism through a five-coordinate trigonal bipyramidal intermediate. The rate law has two terms, rate = (k₁ + k₂[Y])[complex]: k₂ for direct attack by Y, and k₁ for a path in which solvent attacks first and Y then displaces the solvent. The rate depends strongly on the entering group (soft nucleophiles such as I⁻ and PR₃ are fast). Negative activation entropies and volumes support associative attack. Pt(II) complexes are about 10⁵ times less labile than Pd(II) ones, which is why the Pt drug cisplatin reacts slowly enough to be given intact.
A ligand in a square planar complex directs the substitution of the ligand trans to it. This **trans effect** gives the order:

body.eq: CN⁻, CO, C₂H₄ > PR₃, H⁻ > CH₃⁻, SC(NH₂)₂ > C₆H₅⁻, SCN⁻, I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > py, NH₃ > OH⁻ > H₂O

body: Two effects contribute. A strong σ-donor (H⁻, CH₃⁻) weakens the bond trans to it in the ground state; this is the **trans influence** (a thermodynamic property, seen in bond lengths and IR and NMR coupling constants). A good π-acceptor (CO, C₂H₄, CN⁻) stabilizes the five-coordinate transition state by withdrawing electron density from the metal; this effect is kinetic. The trans effect is the basis of the selective synthesis of isomers:

example.title: Cisplatin and transplatin
solution: **Cis**: start from [PtCl₄]²⁻ and add NH₃. The first NH₃ replaces a chloride to give [Pt(NH₃)Cl₃]⁻. In this complex, the chloride trans to Cl is more labile than the chloride trans to NH₃, since Cl⁻ has a higher trans effect than NH₃, so the second NH₃ replaces a chloride trans to a chloride and ends up cis to the first NH₃: cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂].
**Trans**: start from [Pt(NH₃)₄]²⁺ and add Cl⁻. The first Cl⁻ gives [Pt(NH₃)₃Cl]⁺. Now the NH₃ trans to Cl⁻ is the most labile, so the second Cl⁻ enters trans to the first: trans-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂].

sections.title: Electron-transfer reactions
body: Electron transfer between two complexes can occur by two mechanisms.

list: **Outer-sphere**: the coordination spheres of the two complexes stay intact, and the electron tunnels from one to the other as they collide. It dominates when both partners are substitution-inert, as in [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ + [IrCl₆]²⁻ → [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ + [IrCl₆]³⁻.

**Inner-sphere**: a ligand bridges the two metal centers in the transition state, and electron transfer occurs through it. Taube’s classic experiment (Nobel Prize 1983) used [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺ (inert Co(III)) and [Cr(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (labile Cr(II)). The chloride bridges the two metals, the electron moves, and the products are [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ and [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]²⁺, in which the chloride has transferred to Cr. This is inert Cr(III), so the transfer of Cl is proof of the bridge.

body: The rate depends on how much the nuclei must rearrange before the electron can jump, since the electron moves much faster than the nuclei (Franck–Condon principle). Marcus theory (Nobel Prize 1992) gives the activation energy in terms of the **reorganization energy** λ, the energy to distort the reactants and solvent into the geometry of the products without electron transfer. Reactions are slow when the bond lengths differ widely between oxidation states: the Co(III)/Co(II) self-exchange between low-spin t₂g⁶ and high-spin t₂g⁵e_g² is very slow because Co–N lengthens by 0.18 Å (k ≈ 10⁻⁹ M⁻¹ s⁻¹), but [Ru(NH₃)₆]³⁺/²⁺ (both t₂g, 0.04 Å change) exchanges at 10⁴ M⁻¹ s⁻¹.
The **Marcus cross relation** predicts the rate of a cross reaction from the self-exchange rate constants k₁₁ and k₂₂ of the two couples and the equilibrium constant K₁₂ of the cross reaction:

body.eq: k₁₂ = √(k₁₁ k₂₂ K₁₂ f₁₂)     (f₁₂ ≈ 1 when K₁₂ is not too large)

body: A surprise of the theory is the **inverted region**: when the reaction is so exergonic that −ΔG° exceeds λ, the rate falls with increasing driving force. It was confirmed experimentally in 1984 and is important for photosynthesis and solar-energy conversion, since it keeps back-electron transfer slow.

example.problem: Two couples have self-exchange rate constants k₁₁ = 10² and k₂₂ = 10⁴ M⁻¹ s⁻¹, and the cross reaction has K₁₂ = 10⁶. Estimate k₁₂.

check.q: What was the evidence for the inner-sphere mechanism in Taube’s experiment?
check.a: Chloride was transferred to the inert Cr(III) product

check.q: Why is the Co(III)/Co(II) self-exchange so slow?
check.a: A large change in Co–N bond length between low-spin Co(III) and high-spin Co(II)

quiz.q: At 25 °C in 0.1 M solution, a ligand substitution on a complex takes about ten minutes to finish. By Taube’s classification this complex is
quiz.a: Inert, since it is slower than about a minute
wrong: Labile, since the reaction does go to completion
Labile, because any reaction under an hour counts as fast
quiz.why: Labile and inert are purely kinetic labels with a cutoff near one minute; the equilibrium constant is irrelevant to them.

quiz.q: [Ni(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (d⁸) exchanges water over 100 times more slowly than high-spin [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (d⁶). The best explanation is that
quiz.a: Ni²⁺ has a large LFSE, part of which is lost in the transition state
wrong: Ni²⁺ is low spin, which makes it inert
Ni²⁺ is Jahn–Teller distorted, which strengthens its axial bonds
Ni–O bonds are covalent, so they cannot break
quiz.why: Octahedral d⁸ has LFSE of −1.2Δₒ, so it pays a ligand field activation energy. Water-exchange is still fast enough (3 × 10⁴ s⁻¹) for the ion to count as labile, and d⁸ aqua ions are high spin.

quiz.q: In ligand field terms, the ligand field activation energy is
quiz.a: The LFSE lost when the octahedral complex becomes a five- or seven-coordinate transition state
wrong: The energy required to promote an electron from the t₂g to the e_g level
The energy of the metal–ligand bond that has to break in the slow step
The Jahn–Teller stabilization energy of the distorted ground state
quiz.why: It is the change in LFSE between ground state and transition state, which explains why d³ and low-spin d⁶ are inert. Bond energy and electron promotion are different quantities.

quiz.q: Which ion forms the most inert octahedral aqua complex?
quiz.why: Ir³⁺ is low-spin d⁶ and a 5d metal, so it has both a large LFSE and a large Δ. High-spin d⁵, d⁹ and d¹⁰ ions are labile.

quiz.q: Which feature defines an interchange mechanism?
quiz.a: No detectable intermediate; the entering and leaving groups swap in one step within an outer-sphere pair
wrong: A five-coordinate intermediate forms before the entering group binds
A seven-coordinate intermediate forms before the leaving group departs
The metal changes its oxidation state during the swap
quiz.why: Intermediates of lower or higher coordination number characterize D and A. In I, bond making and breaking are concerted, and the leading one gives Iₐ or I_d.

quiz.q: In an Eigen–Wilkins reaction, k = 2 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ and K_os = 5 M⁻¹. At [Y] = 0.20 M, k_obs is
quiz.why: K_os[Y] = 1, so k_obs = k(1)/(1 + 1) = k/2. Quoting k itself assumes saturation, which is only reached when K_os[Y] ≫ 1.

quiz.q: For a reaction with k_obs = kK_os[Y]/(1 + K_os[Y]), a plot of 1/k_obs against 1/[Y] is linear. Its intercept on the 1/k_obs axis is
quiz.why: Inverting gives 1/k_obs = 1/k + 1/(kK_os[Y]). The slope is 1/(kK_os), and the intercept, the high-[Y] limit, is 1/k.

quiz.q: The rate of base hydrolysis of [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺ is first order in OH⁻, yet OH⁻ does not bind cobalt in the slow step. Why is OH⁻ in the rate law?
quiz.a: It deprotonates a coordinated NH₃ in a fast equilibrium to make an amido conjugate base that loses Cl⁻
wrong: It attacks Co associatively to make a seven-coordinate intermediate
It displaces Cl⁻ in an outer-sphere electron transfer
It reduces Co(III) to the labile Co(II), which loses Cl⁻
quiz.why: The amido ligand is a strong π-donor that labilizes the chloride. OH⁻ only appears in the rate law because it generates the reactive conjugate base.

quiz.q: Which complex should NOT undergo SN1CB base hydrolysis?
quiz.why: SN1CB needs a coordinated N–H to deprotonate. NH₃ and ethylenediamine have N–H bonds; the pyridine nitrogen has none.

quiz.q: A square planar Pt(II) complex follows rate = (k₁ + k₂[Y])[complex], with k₁ = 4 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and k₂ = 0.50 M⁻¹ s⁻¹. At [Y] = 0.020 M the pseudo-first-order rate constant is
quiz.why: The two pathways add: 4 × 10⁻³ + 0.50 × 0.020 = 4 × 10⁻³ + 1.0 × 10⁻² = 1.4 × 10⁻² s⁻¹. Dropping the solvent path gives 1.0 × 10⁻²; multiplying the constants has no basis.

quiz.q: Pt(II) complexes substitute about 10⁵ times more slowly than the Pd(II) analogues. What does this mean for cisplatin?
quiz.a: It reacts slowly enough to be administered intact
wrong: It dissolves in water without reacting at all
It must be made by dissociative rather than associative substitution
It is thermodynamically stable toward all substitution
quiz.why: Slow substitution is a kinetic property. Cisplatin does exchange chloride eventually, but over hours rather than milliseconds, and it is not thermodynamically inert.

quiz.q: One equivalent of I⁻ is added to [Pt(NH₃)Cl₃]⁻ (trans effect I⁻ > Cl⁻ > NH₃). Where does the iodide enter?
quiz.a: In place of a chloride trans to the other chloride, so I⁻ ends up cis to NH₃
wrong: In place of the chloride trans to NH₃, so I⁻ ends up trans to NH₃
In place of NH₃, since it has the weakest trans effect
As a fifth ligand, giving a stable five-coordinate Pt(II) complex
quiz.why: The chloride opposite another chloride is the more labile one, because Cl⁻ has a greater trans effect than NH₃. The ligand with the weaker trans effect is not the one lost.

quiz.q: Which statement about the trans effect and trans influence is FALSE?
quiz.a: The trans effect is the same ground-state bond weakening as the trans influence
wrong: A π-acceptor such as C₂H₄ speeds substitution trans to it by stabilizing the five-coordinate transition state
A strong σ-donor such as H⁻ weakens the bond trans to it in the ground state
Adding ligands in a chosen order can give the cis or trans isomer from the same metal
quiz.why: The trans influence is thermodynamic (a ground-state bond length or coupling constant), whereas the trans effect is kinetic and concerns the rate of substitution trans to a ligand.

quiz.q: Why must the reductant be labile in an inner-sphere reaction such as Cr²⁺ + [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺?
quiz.a: It must quickly open a coordination site to bind the bridging ligand
wrong: It must supply the electron, so it needs a very low ionization energy
It lowers the reorganization energy of the oxidant by exchanging ligands
Inert complexes cannot carry any ligand to a bridging position
quiz.why: The bridge forms only if one partner can lose a ligand (here water from high-spin d⁴ Cr²⁺) to bind the chloride on the inert partner. Being labile is not about electron donation.

quiz.q: In Taube’s experiment the product [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]²⁺ keeps its chloride. Why does the chloride stay bound?
wrong: Cr(III) is a Jahn–Teller d⁴ ion with strong axial bonds to the ligands
Chloride lies trans to a water ligand, which blocks its loss from the metal
The Cr–Cl bond is thermodynamically stronger than any Cr–O bond in the complex
quiz.why: d³ has a large ligand field activation energy, so the Cr–Cl bond is not broken on the experiment’s timescale. That kinetic inertness is what makes the transferred chloride visible.

quiz.q: Two couples have self-exchange constants k₁₁ = 25 and k₂₂ = 1 × 10⁴ M⁻¹ s⁻¹. Their cross reaction has K₁₂ = 4 × 10². With f₁₂ ≈ 1, the Marcus cross relation gives k₁₂ as
quiz.why: k₁₂ = (25 × 10⁴ × 400)^{1/2} = (10⁸)^{1/2} = 10⁴. Omitting the square root gives 10⁸; leaving out K₁₂ gives 500.

quiz.q: In Marcus theory, the reorganization energy λ is
quiz.a: The energy to distort reactants and solvent into the product geometry without transferring the electron
wrong: The free energy change ΔG° of the electron-transfer reaction
The energy needed to remove an electron from the donor
The activation energy for substituting a ligand on the donor
quiz.why: Because the electron moves much faster than the nuclei (Franck–Condon), the nuclei must first rearrange, and λ measures the cost of that rearrangement.

quiz.q: A charge-separated state can fall back to the ground state with a very large driving force, −ΔG° > λ. Marcus theory predicts this back-electron transfer is
quiz.a: Slow, because it lies in the inverted region
wrong: Fast, because the rate always rises with −ΔG°
quiz.why: Once −ΔG° exceeds λ the rate falls with increasing driving force. This slows wasteful back reactions in photosynthesis and solar-energy conversion.

summary: Labile complexes react in under a minute; inert ones are slower. d³ and low-spin d⁶ octahedral complexes, and 4d and 5d metals, are inert. High-spin d⁴ and d⁹ are labile.
Octahedral substitution is usually dissociative interchange, described by the Eigen–Wilkins mechanism. Base hydrolysis of Co(III) ammines follows SN1CB.
Square planar d⁸ complexes react associatively. The trans effect (CN⁻, CO > PR₃ > I⁻ > Cl⁻ > NH₃ > H₂O) controls which isomer forms, as in the syntheses of cis- and transplatin.
Electron transfer is outer-sphere (intact spheres) or inner-sphere (a bridging ligand). Marcus theory links the rate to reorganization energy: k₁₂ = √(k₁₁k₂₂K₁₂f₁₂).

problems.q: Explain why [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ exchanges water over days while [Cr(H₂O)₆]²⁺ exchanges almost instantly.
problems.solution: Cr(III) is d³: t₂g³ gives a large LFSE (−1.2Δₒ) that is lost in the transition state, so substitution is slow. Cr(II) is high-spin d⁴ with an e_g electron, so it is Jahn–Teller distorted, with weak axial bonds, and has little LFSE (−0.6Δₒ) to lose: labile.
problems.a: Cr(III) d³ has a large ligand field activation energy; Cr(II) is Jahn–Teller distorted.

problems.q: How would you prepare cis-[PtCl₂(NH₃)(py)] from [PtCl₄]²⁻, and why do NH₃ and pyridine end up cis?
problems.solution: Add one equivalent of NH₃ to [PtCl₄]²⁻ to give [Pt(NH₃)Cl₃]⁻. In this complex the chloride trans to another chloride is more labile than the chloride trans to NH₃, because Cl⁻ has a larger trans effect than NH₃. Pyridine therefore replaces a chloride that is trans to chloride, and it ends up cis to the NH₃.
problems.a: Add NH₃ first, then pyridine; the trans effect of Cl⁻ directs the pyridine cis to NH₃.

problems.q: A substitution of X by Y in an octahedral complex shows the rate = k_obs[complex], with k_obs the same for three different entering groups Y. What mechanism is suggested?
problems.solution: The rate does not depend on the entering group, so bond breaking to the leaving group controls the rate: a dissociative (D) or dissociative interchange (I_d) mechanism.
